result:
There's a strange kind of paralysis that comes when someone tells you, "write freely about whatever you want."

For years, almost everything we write is prompted. Write an essay about the causes of World War I. Write a cover letter explaining why you're perfect for this job. Write a caption for this photo. The assignment gives you walls to push against. But when the walls are taken away and you're left standing in an open field, you don't know which direction to walk.

So I’ll start here, in the open field.

I want to write about small rooms.

Not in the architectural sense, although I love those too — the window seat that is exactly one person wide, the kitchen nook where two mugs can steam next to each other without any extra space left over. I mean the small rooms we make inside our own lives. The rituals that are so contained, so specific, that they become a kind of home.

For me, one of those rooms is the hour just before the world wakes up. Not quite morning, not quite night. If you live in a city, it's the hour when the delivery trucks start to hiss down the street but no one has turned their kitchen light on yet. If you live somewhere quieter, it's when the birds haven't decided if they mean it. I like that hour because no one wants anything from you yet. Your phone, if you let it, is still asleep. No one has asked you a question. No one is waiting for a reply.

In that hour, I have a ritual that is almost embarrassingly simple: I make coffee, I open the window even if it's cold, and I sit with a notebook. Not to be productive. Not to journal with intent or manifest or do morning pages the correct way. Just to see what’s there. Some days what’s there is a grocery list. Some days it’s a line I heard three years ago that finally makes sense. Some days it’s just, *I am tired and I don’t know why.* The point was never to produce something. The point was to have a small room to sit in before the big house of the day opens all its doors.

I think we undervalue small rooms. We live in a culture that is obsessed with scale. Scale your business, scale your audience, scale your impact. We are taught to think that bigger is more real. A viral post is more real than a note slipped to a friend. A stadium tour is more real than someone playing guitar in their kitchen. But most of our lives are not lived at scale. They are lived in these tiny, unscalable moments that will never be seen by anyone else and will never matter to history, and yet they are somehow the entire fabric of what it feels like to be alive.

Here is another small room: the way a library smells in late August. Or the way your favorite sweater has worn thin at the cuffs. Or the particular way your best friend texts you — maybe they always send a follow-up message that just says “anyway!!” after a long story. These things are not important. If you tried to explain to a stranger why they matter, you would sound ridiculous. But they are the reason you know you are you. Identity isn’t really built out of big milestones. It’s built out of these tiny, repeated textures.

I used to think that freedom meant having infinite options. That to be free was to keep every door open. If I could just keep all possibilities alive — live in any city, become any kind of person, never close anything off — then I would finally feel free. It took me a long time to realize that infinite options is not freedom, it’s vertigo. It’s standing in that open field again, paralyzed.

Real freedom, I’ve come to think, is the ability to choose your constraints and then love them. To choose the small room and then decorate it with obsessive care. The novelist who decides *I will write only about one town in Dublin on one day in 1904* has not limited herself. She has given herself a world deep enough to actually get lost in. The painter who decides *I will only use blue for a year* hasn’t narrowed his vision; he has finally learned to *see* blue. The person who decides *I will walk the same route every morning* starts to notice that the route is never the same at all — the light, the cracks in the sidewalk, the cat that only appears on Thursdays.

Constraints are not the opposite of creativity. They are the engine of it.

This is why I love the idea of a “practice.” Not a performance, not a product. A practice is something you return to whether it was good today or not. You practice piano. You practice meditation. You practice kindness. No one asks if you “finished” practicing. You just go back to the room.

We have lost a lot of practices and replaced them with content. We don’t practice photography anymore; we produce images for a feed that must constantly be fed. We don’t practice writing; we produce takes. We don’t practice friendship; we produce engagement. Content wants to be big and fast and seen. Practice wants to be small and slow and repeated. Content asks, “How did it perform?” Practice asks, “Did you show up?”

If you are feeling anxious or scattered or strangely empty despite being very busy, I wonder if it might be because you have a lot of content in your life and not enough practice. Not enough small rooms.

So here is an invitation, not an assignment: build one small room this week.

It doesn’t have to be impressive. It could be ten minutes in the morning with tea and no phone. It could be that you decide to learn how to make one soup, really well, and you make it every Sunday in October. It could be that you write one sentence a day in a notebook that no one will ever read. It could be that you sit on the same bench in the park for five minutes after work and just notice what’s changed.

The rules for a small room are simple:

1. It should be small enough that you can do it even on a bad day.
2. It should be repeatable.
3. It should not need to be shared to be valid.
4. You should be allowed to do it badly.

That last one is crucial. The small room is not where you go to be good. It’s where you go to be.

There is a Japanese concept I think about a lot called *wabi-sabi*, which finds beauty in imperfection and impermanence. A cracked bowl repaired with gold. The uneven glaze on a handmade cup. We intuitively understand this beauty when we see it in objects, but we rarely extend it to our own lives. We want our lives to be seamless, cracked-free, perfectly glazed. But a life without cracks has no place for the gold to go.

Your small room will be imperfect. You will miss days. You will sit down to write and write nothing. You will make the soup too salty. That is not failure. That is the texture that tells you it’s real and it’s yours.

A few years ago I started keeping a list, not of accomplishments or goals, but of tiny things that made me feel briefly, uncomplicatedly, alive. The list lives on a folded piece of paper in my wallet and it says things like:

*The sound of wind in the pines behind the supermarket.*
*The first sip of water when you are really thirsty.*
*Finding a book with someone else’s notes in the margins and realizing you agree with them.*
*When someone remembers how you take your coffee after only being told once.*
*Late afternoon light on a wooden floor.*

None of these things will change the world. But they have completely changed my *experience* of the world, because once you start noticing them, they appear everywhere. Attention is a kind of alchemy. What you pay attention to, grows.

And perhaps that is the real reason to build small rooms: they train your attention. They teach you how to look. In a world that is constantly trying to direct your gaze outward — look at this crisis, look at this product, look at this person who is more successful/thinner/happier than you — a practice quietly says, look *here*. Look at this one small, ordinary thing until it reveals itself to be extraordinary.

You do not need to blow up your life to find meaning. You don’t need to quit your job and move to a cabin or have a grand revelation. You just need to look more closely at the life you already have. The holy is not hidden. It’s just small. It’s waiting in the window seat, in the kitchen nook, in the hour before the world wakes up, with a notebook open and coffee getting cold and nowhere else you need to be.

If you’ve read this far, thank you for sitting in this small room with me for a little while. It was nice to share it with you.

Now go make your own.
